title: Immune-Related Meningoencephalitis following Nivolumab in Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old African-American man with a 4-year history of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma presented with a 1-week history of bilateral lower extremity weakness, lethargy, several falls, hyperthermia, confusion, and gait abnormalities. His cancer history included a partial nephrectomy for papillary RCC with clear cell component, excisional biopsy confirming metastatic CCRCC, treatment with pazopanib and sunitinib, and ultimately a left radical nephrectomy. A positive QuantiFERON TB Gold test had excluded him from earlier immunotherapy trials. He then received seven cycles of nivolumab (240 mg) without prior complications.

On this admission, he became hypothermic, was transferred to the ICU, and required endotracheal intubation. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a lymphocytic pleocytosis (white blood cell count 27/mm3, 78% lymphocytes; protein 70 mg/dL). CSF virus culture and Gram stain showed no growth; a CSF pathogen panel and cryptococcal antigen were negative. Blood cultures and AFB smear were negative. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and a 1.7 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm focus of T1-hypointensity at the midbrain–pons junction that had been stable for four years. A CSF MTB PCR test was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Disease progression — “Special attention should rule out other conditions that may cause neurological impairment such as disease progression, seizure activity, infection (in particular herpes simplex virus), and metabolic alterations.”  
2. Seizure activity — “it was thought that his hyperthermia may have been due to a diencephalic seizure.”  
3. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis — “A CSF virus culture and gram stain demonstrated no growth, the CSF pathogen panel was negative…”  
4. Cryptococcal meningitis — “the cryptococcal antigen was negative.”  
5. Tuberculous meningitis — “The MTB polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test was negative.”  
6. Aseptic meningitis — “Patients with these conditions may present with headaches, vomiting, and fever; however, patients with aseptic meningitis often have a normal mental status unlike immune-related encephalitis.”  
7. Drug-induced meningitis — “Considering that our patient was not on any of these drugs, this diagnosis may be ruled out.”  
8. Tuberculoma — “the left midbrain/pons lesion was unlikely to be a tuberculoma as the mass had been present for 4 years without changes and remained unchanged for the next several years after receiving treatment for latent TB.”  
9. Immune-related meningoencephalitis — “This diagnosis was further substantiated by clinical improvement with immunosuppression and lack of empiric antibiotic therapy for meningoencephalitis.”
